m2c/src/m2c/sandbox -- Patch C11a: the command sandbox (bubblewrap).

SECURITY-CRITICAL.  Four small modules, each with its own long docstring:

``profile``  builds the bubblewrap argument list: what is mounted, read-only or writable, which
             namespaces are new, what environment the command gets.  A pure function.
``bwrap``    finds bubblewrap and a shell and builds the full command, ``[bwrap, *profile, "--",
             shell, "-c", command]``.  ``tools/shell.py`` runs it like it ran ``[shell, "-c", command]``.
``probe``    really tests the sandbox (a throw-away project and home with canaries, eleven
             escape attempts) and returns a structured result.
``__init__`` (this file) the three questions the rest of m2c asks:

* ``get_status()``  is a working sandbox available?  Answers from the probe, run once per session per
  settings and remembered.  ``available`` is True only when EVERY check passed; nothing else may
  call the sandbox active.
* ``is_available()``  the same as a bool.
* ``fresh_probe()``  a new probe that ignores the cache (the doctor's).

The rule everything here follows: the sandbox is never assumed.  If it was not seen to hold, the
status says so, with a fixed reason, and callers must say "full privileges" and mean it.

m2c/src/m2c/sandbox/bridge.py -- Patch C11b: the bridge that gives a sandboxed command a proxy to talk to.

WHAT THIS FILE IS
-----------------
C11a runs a shell command in a bubblewrap sandbox whose network namespace is UNSHARED: the command has loopback and
nothing else.  C11b gives it *controlled* network without ever giving it a network:

    command --HTTP CONNECT--> 127.0.0.1:3128 (this bridge, inside the sandbox)
            --unix socket---> proxy on the host (netproxy.py), which decides, resolves, pins and connects.

The bridge is deliberately dumb.  It relays bytes between a TCP connection on the sandbox's own loopback and the unix
socket that the host proxy listens on.  It decides nothing, reads nothing and logs nothing; every decision is made by
the proxy on the host, so a command that talks to the unix socket directly, or kills the bridge and starts its own,
gains nothing.  A program that ignores the proxy settings simply cannot connect: there is no route (fail closed by
construction).

TWO ROLES IN ONE FILE
---------------------
* As a MODULE (imported by m2c): the constants, ``NetworkMount``, ``proxy_environment`` / ``apply_proxy_environment``
  (the variables injected into the command's environment AFTER sanitizing) and ``launcher_argv``.
* As a SCRIPT (copied by the proxy into its private directory, mounted read-only into the sandbox and run by the
  system ``python3`` there):  ``python3 -I bridge.py --port P --sock PATH -- COMMAND...``.  It binds
  127.0.0.1

m2c/src/m2c/sandbox/bwrap.py -- Patch C11a: finding bubblewrap and building the full command.

SECURITY-CRITICAL.  ``profile.build_profile`` says WHAT the sandbox is; this module says how to
start it.  ``tools/shell.py`` calls ``wrap_command`` and runs what it returns exactly as it ran
``[shell, "-c", command]`` before: the same ``subprocess.Popen`` with ``start_new_session=True``,
so C07's process-group kill, timeout, cancel, streaming and output cap are untouched.  Why that
still works: the process the shell tool signals is bubblewrap itself, the leader of the new
session; bubblewrap is also PID 1's parent, and when it dies (SIGKILL included) the kernel kills
every process in the sandbox's PID namespace.  A command that calls ``setsid`` or traps SIGTERM
therefore cannot outlive the call, which is the gap C07 documented and this patch closes.

The command line is ``[bwrap, *profile, "--", shell, "-c", command]``: a list, the command is ONE
element, nothing is quoted or joined, and the double dash makes sure a command that starts with
``-`` is never read as a bubblewrap option.

``find_bwrap`` looks only in ABSOLUTE ``PATH`` entries.  A relative entry (``.``, an empty
element, ``bin``) would let a file in the project directory be found first; a project is the
model's workspace, so it must never be a place a binary is picked up from.

m2c/src/m2c/sandbox/netpolicy.py -- Patch C11b: which domains a sandboxed command may reach (the decision logic).

THE RULES (pure, no I/O except the one saved file)
--------------------------------------------------
The allowlist holds EXACT hosts (``pypi.org``), explicit wildcards (``*.example.com``) and exact IP literals.

* A wildcard matches any host UNDER the name, at any depth, and never the bare name: ``*.example.com`` matches
  ``a.example.com`` and ``a.b.example.com`` but not ``example.com``.  A wildcard needs at least two labels after the
  star (``*.com`` is ignored), and nothing else with a star is valid.  The star cannot know public suffixes, so a
  person who writes ``*.co.uk`` has allowed a lot; that is theirs to decide.
* Names are lowercased, IDNA-normalized (what is shown and compared is the ASCII/punycode form, so a look-alike
  domain in another script can never be mistaken for the real one on screen) and have no trailing dot.
* IP literals are DENIED unless the exact address is listed (never asked about).  Odd spellings of an address
  (``2130706433``, ``0x7f.1``, ``127.1``) are denied outright.  ``localhost`` and ``*.localhost`` are denied too.
* Only the allowed destination ports pass (443 by default); any other port is denied before anything else.

m2c/src/m2c/sandbox/netproxy.py -- Patch C11b: the host-side proxy that decides where a sandboxed command may connect.

THE DESIGN
----------
The sandbox keeps NO direct network (``--unshare-net`` stays).  On the host an asyncio proxy listens on a UNIX socket
inside a private temporary directory (mode 0700, owned by the user).  That directory is bind-mounted READ-ONLY into
the sandbox together with ``bridge.py``; inside, the bridge relays 127.0.0.1:3128 to the socket.  A program that
ignores the proxy settings cannot connect at all: fail closed by construction.  Everything that matters is decided
HERE, on the host, where the command cannot reach the code or its memory.

WHAT THE PROXY DOES, per connection
-----------------------------------
1. Reads the request head (request line and headers up to the blank line) under a total deadline and size caps
   (slowloris and oversized-header protection).  It looks at the request line only; headers are skipped, never
   parsed, stored or logged, and the payload that follows is never looked at.
2. Accepts ``CONNECT host:port`` only.  Plain ``http://`` requests get a fixed 403 (cleartext is OFF by default;
   ``ProxyConfig.allow_cleartext`` turns it on, and then the proxy reads the host out of the request line, nothing
   else, and tunnels the rest blindly).  Every other method gets a fixed 405.
3. Asks the policy (netpolicy.py): allowlist, ports (443 only by default), IP literals, the person's prompt.

m2c/src/m2c/sandbox/probe.py -- Patch C11a: the sandbox self-test.

SECURITY-CRITICAL.  "bubblewrap is installed" proves nothing: a kernel that forbids user
namespaces, a container that cannot mount ``/proc``, an AppArmor rule or one wrong option all
leave a ``bwrap`` binary that either refuses to start or starts and confines nothing.  So the
rule of this package is: the sandbox is "active" only after it has been seen to HOLD.  This
module is the seeing.

What it does.  ``run_probe`` builds a throw-away world in a temporary directory: a FAKE HOME
with canaries in ``.ssh``, ``.aws`` and ``.bashrc``, and a FAKE PROJECT inside it with
``.git``, ``.m2c``, ``.bashrc`` and ``.profile``.  Then, with the SAME profile the shell tool
uses (``profile.build_profile``, the same toolchain and extra read-only settings), it starts
one bubblewrap per check, each running a small POSIX script that tries to do something the
sandbox must prevent, and judges the result from two independent sources: what the script
printed AND what is on the real disk afterwards (a write that "failed" quietly but happened is
caught; so is an escape that printed nothing).

The checks (``CHECK_NAMES``; each is one run):

``basic``                a normal command works: ``echo`` and writing a file inside the project.
``write_outside_project``  writes to the home, ``/usr``, ``/etc``, ``/`` and ``..`` all fail.
``write_git``            nothing can be added to, appended to, moved out of, or removed from ``.git``.
``write

m2c/src/m2c/sandbox/profile.py -- Patch C11a: the bubblewrap profile.

SECURITY-CRITICAL.  ``build_profile`` turns "run a command for this project" into the
list of ``bwrap`` options that confine it.  It is a pure function: it looks at the
disk (to see what exists) and starts nothing, so every property below is testable on
a machine without bubblewrap.  What it returns is ARGV, a list of strings, never a
shell string: nothing here is ever joined, quoted or parsed by a shell.

What the sandbox is
-------------------
A new root filesystem (a tmpfs bubblewrap makes), into which these are mounted, in
this order (a LATER mount wins over an earlier one at the same place, which is why
the order is part of the contract and tests pin it):

1.  ``/usr`` read-only; ``/bin``, ``/sbin``, ``/lib``, ``/lib64`` as symlinks into
    it when the machine has the merged-``/usr`` layout, as read-only binds of the
    real directory when it does not (``SystemLayout``).
2.  A short, explicit list of ``/etc`` entries (``ETC_ENTRIES``), read-only, each
    only if it exists: passwd, group, ld.so.cache, alternatives, certificates and a
    few more.  NOT ``/etc`` as a whole: ``shadow``, ``ssh``, ``ssl/private`` and
    the system start-up files are simply not there.
3.  A minimal ``/proc`` (of the new PID namespace, so the host's processes are not
    in it), a minimal ``/dev``, and a private, empty, writable ``/tmp``.
4.  The home directory, as an EMPTY tmpfs, made read-only at the end.  The home
